newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks seen lower at start.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks seen lower at start.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to head lower at the start Thursday as the market continues to correct ahead of next week's FOMC meeting.
"We are digesting $4 trillion in gains in a market which has been rallying for 28 months," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities.

"There has to be a period of consolidation. We are going through a correction which encompasses the big gainers like the high techs and the interest sensitive stocks. It's more than a one day affair."
"The immediate problem is to find a bottom for the techs and see to what extent the market has discounted Fed tightening," Wachtel said.
Next week's meeting of the Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committe has cast a shadow over trading as investors try to gauge Fed action on interest ratres.
Stocks are still in a bull market, Wachtel said.

"It's a bull market as long as profits justify multiples, the long bond yield doesn't reach 7.25 or 7.50 percent, at which point people will move money from stocks to bonds and mutual fund flows stay at $15 billion to $20 billion a month."
The Tokyo stock market is closed for a national holiday Thursday. Trade will resume Friday.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 39.6 at 4292.6.

Among U.S. shares traded in London, Microsoft Corp, which dropped $2-1/4 in New York on Wednesday, was up $1/4 to $97-5/8 after news that Hewlett-Packard had jumped solidly in the Microsoft Windows NT camp.
Hewlett, up $3/4 to $56-1/8, said on Wednesday it would "aggressively integrate" Microsoft's operating system into its computers. International Business Machines Corp was up $3/8 to $138-3/4.
The dollar ended its Asia session slightly firmer against the mark and was off its lows in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were thinly mixed, with the long bond up 1/32 to yield 6.98 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that the rapidly unfolding deregulation and consolidation of the utility industry is spawning a profusion of takeover deals among retail, wholesale, regional and national power providers.

The New York Times Market Place writes that Luby's Cafeterias Inc did not higher an outside auditor to make sure its books were in order after its chief executive officer committed suicide and its chairman retired.
